entries.title: Psalms 138:1
segments:
We have here the first of eight psalms composed by David and arranged together near the close of the book of Psalms.  The first two celebrate the glorious attributes of God as manifested in his dealings with the psalmist; the next four are prayers for deliverance in the midst of deep distress; then follow two closing psalms, in the first of which he anticipates, in the language of triumph, a complete victory over all his foes, and in the second celebrates the goodness of God after this victory is now achieved. 
 
  Before the gods; probably, in the face of all false gods. 
 
Every new mercy should excite us to new gratitude and praise; and on all suitable occasions we should publicly acknowledge God's goodness to us.

entries.title: Psalms 138:2
segments:
Thy word; thy word of promise. 
 
  Above all thy name; above all hitherto known of thy perfections. The name of God is the sum of his perfections as they are manifested to us. 
 
God will more than fulfil the highest expectations of all who put their trust in him.

entries.title: Psalms 138:3
segments: God's servants never ask help from him in vain.

entries.title: Psalms 138:5
segments: The Old Testament prophets rightly anticipated the conversion of all nations as the final result of what God did for his ancient people.

entries.title: Psalms 138:6
segments: Nothing brings us so near to God as humility; nothing removes us so far from him as pride.

entries.title: Psalms 138:7
segments: Though God often suffers his people to be troubled by their enemies, he does not allow them to be destroyed.  He will interpose at the right time for their salvation and for the shame of their persecutors.

entries.title: Psalms 138:8
segments:
Forsake not the works of thine own hands; the works of mercy which thou hast begun in my behalf, carry on to completion. 
 
God would have us urge his past mercies towards us as an argument why he should bestow more.
